newsitem.title: ECUADOR: Ecuador's Bucaram defies congressional ouster.
newsitem.headline: Ecuador's Bucaram defies congressional ouster.

text.p: The military looked set to become Ecuador's final arbiter of power on Friday after Congress voted to oust President Abdala Bucaram and he defiantly pledged to see out his full term of office.

Bucaram, flanked by troops as he gave a brief statement to reporters outside the presidential palace, called the 44-34 vote by Congress deposing him an act of "judicial barbarity" and said he had no intention of leaving the job he was democratically elected to just six months ago.
"The power of businessmen and the power of bankers ... will never be as powerful as the constitution," he said, suggesting the bid to depose him had been engineered by Ecuador's economic elite.
"I am the only president elected by the poor and people of Ecuador," he added.

After its summary vote to impeach Bucaram, Congress moved hastily to swear in its leader, Fabian Alarcon, as interim president. But Bucaram dismissed him as a member of a "congressional dictatorship" responsible for an "anti-democratic" grab for the reins of power.
A quirky populist known as "El Loco", or "Madman," Bucaram took office promising to be the president of Ecuador's vast army of poor.

But his ouster by Congress, on grounds of mental incompetence, came after the country was shut down on Wednesday and Thursday by a massive 48-hour nationwide strike to protest draconian economic belt-tighening measures his government clamped on Ecuador in early January.

The measures, coupled with what many regard as Bucaram's often outlandish behaviour since taking office, drove his approval rating down almost as quickly as the cost of living shot up. They included electricity and gas rate hikes totalling more than 200 percent and a 60 percent rise in bus fares.
Bucaram appealed directly for military support late on Thursday in a statement issued by his press spokesman after his formal ouster by Congress.

There was no immediate response from army leaders, who restored democratic rule in Ecuador in August 1979, but military commanders entered the presidential palace shortly after 1 a.m. (0600 GMT) and political commentators said they were likely to seek a negotiated settlement of the crisis sparked by his continuing fight for political survival.

Shortly before the meeting began, troops ringing the palace used tear gas and fired a burst of rifle shots into the air to disperse scores of angry demonstrators insisting on Bucaram's immediate removal from power.

Ecuador's constitution is extremely vague on who should replace a sitting president and it was not immediately clear if Bucaram, or anyone else could mount a serious legal challenge to Alarcon's appointment as acting president until August 1998.

A statement issued by the military high command shortly before the meeting at the presidential palace said Vice President Rosalia Arteaga had signed a decree, apparently after the tumultuous session in Congress, naming herself as president.
"There is serious judicial confusion," the military statement said.
